 Meeting Schedule

The regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month,
closed session business will usually commence at 5:30 p.m., when scheduled, and general business
session will commence at 6:30 p.m.

Brown Act

Agendas are drafted to accurately state what the legislative body is being asked to consider. The
legislative body can take action on "all items" listed on the agenda and be in compliance with the open
meeting laws. Under the Brown Act, no action may be taken on a matter unless it is listed on the
agenda, or unless certain emergency or special circumstances exist. The governing body may direct
staff to investigate and/or schedule certain matters for consideration at a future meeting.

City's Vision Statement

Coming Soon

Public Communications

Public Comments on agenda items are limited to three (3) minutes. All comments are to be addressed
directly to the Agency Members not to the members of the public.

Emails for public comment received prior to 12pm on the day of the Council Meeting will be summarized
by the City Clerk, not read in its entirety. A copy of the email will be provided to the City Council and will
also be available at the City Clerk's Office for public review. A copy of each email will be recorded for
public record and noted on the official minutes of tonight's meeting.

Meeting Compensation Disclosure
Pursuant to Government Code Section 54952.3: Disclosure of compensation for meeting
attendance by City Council Members is $650 monthly regardless of the amount of meetings.

Comments From The Audience - Non-Agenda Items
During this time, members of the public may address the City Council regarding any items not
listed on the agenda and within the subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council and not on
this agenda. Comments from the audience will be limited to three (3) minutes per speaker;
unless authorized by the Mayor, the time limit may not be extended by utilizing another
member's time. There will be no debate or action on items not listed on the agenda unless
authorized by law. The collective initial period of time for comments from the audience shall
be limited to 45 minutes. Any speaker that did not get a chance to speak during this segment
due to the 45-minute limitations will be able to speak at the end of the meeting prior to
adjournment.

Note: The City Council desires to provide all members of the public with the opportunity to
address the Council. Nevertheless, obscene language, comments intended to
disrupt/interfere, other actions which disrupt the progress of the meeting or slanderous
comments will not be tolerated and may result in ejection and/or may constitute a violation of
South Gate Municipal Code Section1.04.110.

Reports And Comments From City Officials
During this time, members of the City Council will report on matters pertaining to their service
on various intergovernmental boards and commissions as a representative of the City
pursuant to Assembly Bill 1234. City Council Members will also have an opportunity to
comment on matters not on the agenda.

Consent Calendar Items
Agenda Items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are Consent Calendar Items. All items including
Ordinances, Resolutions and Contracts, may be approved by adoption of the Consent
Calendar, individually and collectively by one (1) motion. There will be no separate discussion
of these items unless Members of the City Council, the public, or staff request that specific
items be removed from the Consent Calendar for separate discussion and action. Members
of the public are permitted to speak on any item listed but their time period is limited to three
(3) minutes in total.

Any motion to introduce or adopt an Ordinance on the Consent Calendar shall be: (1) a
motion to waive the reading of the Ordinance and introduce the Ordinance or (2) a motion to
waive the reading of the Ordinance and adopt the Ordinance, as appropriate.

GENERAL NOTICE TO THE PUBLIC

The City Council adopted new rules relating to the conduct of the public meetings, proceedings, and
business in the City of South Gate on July 12, 2022, (Resolution 2022-38-CC) and go into effect on
August 1, 2022. Resolution #2022-38-CC is available at the City Clerk’s Office.

MEETING SCHEDULE

Regular meetings of the City Council are held on the second and fourth Tuesday of each month, closed
session meetings will commence at 5:30 p.m. unless posted otherwise on its agenda. The regular City
Council meetings will commence at 6:30 p.m. Agendas are available at the following locations: City Clerk
Office, Public Notice Boards at City Hall, and on the City’s web page at https://www.cityofsouthgate.org

The Public can sign up to receive automatic notices of postings of agendas for the City Council or any
other Commission or Board of the City of South Gate. Visit the City webpage and click on the Agenda &
Minutes icon. That will take you the page where an individual can enter their email in the “Email
Updates” box to register.

  7
 PUBLIC COMMENT/PARTICIPATION

Any person may request to address a legislative body during a public meeting. The Presiding Officer will
call upon those present in the Council Chambers first. After all speakers in the Chambers have spoken,
the Presiding Officer will call upon those participating via zoom or teleconference.

Speakers are limited to three (3) minutes on any item listed on the agenda, including public hearings.
Under Comments from the Audience portion, speakers are also limited to a single three (3) minutes time
limit. Comments from the Audience is initially limited to 45 minutes at each meeting. Any speaker still
wishing to speak, that did not speak, will have an addition Comments from the Audience opportunity after
the last business item is finished. The Presiding Officer may extend the time limit as long as there is no
objection from the City Council as a body.

To ensure that the public is able to participate, the City provides the opportunity to submit their
comments in person, virtually, email, phone call, mail and any other method which may become
available. Methods of participation may be subject to change during other such times when a State of
Emergency, Health Order or State Executive Order limits in-person participation.

CURFEW

In absence of a motion duly adopted by majority vote of the City Council, the Presiding Officer may
adjourn the City Council meetings at 10:30 p.m. The Presiding Officer may ask the City Council if any
agenda items listed should be continued or dealt with during the meeting. For those items to be
continued, the City Council can direct the item be placed on the next City Council agenda or the current
meeting may be adjourned to a time certain at which time the meeting shall be reconvened as an
Adjourned Regular Meeting of the City Council and action upon the published agenda continued.

STAFF REPORTS

As a general rule, staff reports. or other written documentation are prepared/organized with respect to
each item of business listed on the agenda. Meeting agendas and staff reports are available at least 72-
hours prior to the scheduled regular City Council meeting and a minimum of 24-hours prior to a Special
City Council meeting. There are times when the City Council receives written material. revised material
after the posting of agendas, these materials are become a public record and will be available for public
view within 72-hours after the meeting in which they were received. Those materials and any other public
document can be inspected in the City Clerk's Office located at 8650 California Avenue, South Gate.

SERVICES TO FACILITATE ACCESS TO PUBLIC MEETINGS

In compliance with the American with Disabilities Act, if you need special assistance to participate in the
City Council Meetings, please contact the Office of the City Clerk. Notification 48 hours prior to the City
Council Meeting will enable the City to make reasonable arrangements to assure accessibility. For
further information, please contact the Office of the City Clerk at (323) 563-9510 or via email at
yglaze@sogate.org.

 SUBJECT:  CITY  OF  SOUTH  GATE  2022  PUBLIC  HEALTH  GOALS  REPORT  ON
 DRINKING  WATER  QUALITY

 PURPOSE:  The City's  municipal  water  system  must comply  with  the regulatory  requirements
 of the California  Health  and Safety  Code  ("Code").  The 2022  Public  Health  Goals  Report  is
 required  to be filed  by the City  Council  every  three years to comply  with  state law.  The report
 provides  information  on concentration  levels  for certain  constituents  for which  only  public  health
 goals have been set, but do not have established  enforceable  water  quality  standards.

 RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider  following  the conclusion  of
 the public  hearing,  receiving  and filing  the City  of South  Gate 2022  Public  Health  Goals  Report
 to meet the requirements  of the California  Health  and Safety  Code.

 FISCAL  IMPACT:  None;  however,  the  cost  of  preparing  the  2022  Public  Health  Goals
 ("PHG")  Report  was $2,334  and was funded  with  Water  Funds.

 NOTICING  PROCEDURES:  A notice  of the public  hearing  was published  in the South
 Gate Press on November  10, 2022,  and the report  was posted  on the City  website.

 ANALYSIS:  The  City's  municipal  water  system  serves  water  that  meets  state  and  federal
 drinking  water  quality  standards.  Over  2,000  water  samples  are taken  annually  to  confirm
 compliance.  The  South  Gate 2022  PHG  Report  documents  the results  of water  sampling  from
 2019,  2020  and 2021  of five  water  contaminants  for  which  PHG  or Maximum  Contaminant
 Level  Goals  (MCLG)  are established.  PHGs  and MCLGs  are not a water  quality  standard.  They
 are established  goals  that  are not  enforceable.  The  enforceable  water  quality  standard  is the
 Maximum  Contaminant  Level  (MCL).  The  results  in the 2022  PHG  Report  denote  that  the
 detection  levels  of the five  water  contaminants  exceeded  the PHG  and MCLG  Goals  but are
 below  the MCL  thereby  meeting  state and federal  drinking  water  quality  standards.

 According  to the PHG  Report,  costly  treatment  processes  would  be required  to reduce  the levels
  of the constituents  identified  above  as below  the PHG  and MCLG.  The costs to reduce  these
  constituents  to  below  their  PHG  and  MCLG  are  estimated  at $228  to  $1,641  per  service
  connection  per year,  or $3.2  million  to  $23.4 million  per year.  Given  the significant  financial
 burden  on customers,  no treatment  action  is necessary,  required  or proposed  at this time.

1.O  Introduction

Under the Calderon-Sher  Safe Drinking Water Act of 1996 public water systems  in
California  serving  greater  than 10,000  service  connections  must prepare  a report
containing  information  on 1) detection  of any contaminant  in drinking water at a level
exceeding  a Public Health Goal (PHG), 2) estimate  of costs to remove  detected
contaminants  to below the PHG using Best Available Technology  (BAT), and 3) health
risks for each contaminant  exceeding  a PHG.  This report must be made available to
the public every three years.  The initial PHGs Report was due on July 1, 1998, and
subsequent  reports are due every three years thereafter.

The 2022 PHGs Report has been prepared  to address the requirements  set forth in
Section 116470 of the California  Health and Safety Code.  It is based on water quality
analyses during calendar years 2019, 2020, and 2021 or, if certain analyses were not
performed  during those years, the most recent data is used.  The 2022 PHGs Report
has been designed to be as informative  as possible, without unnecessary  duplication of
information  contained  in the Consumer  Confidence  Report (also known  as Water
Quality Report), which was mailed to customers  by July Ist of each year.

There are no regulations  explaining  requirements  for the preparation  of PHGs reports.
A workgroup  of the Association  of California  Water Agencies  (ACWA) Water Quality
Committee  has prepared  suggested  guidelines  for water utilities to use in preparing
PHGs reports.  The ACWA guidelines  were used in the preparation  of this 2022 PHGs
Report.  These guidelines  include tables of cost estimates  for BAT.  The State of
California (State) provides ACWA with numerical health risks and category of health risk
information  for contaminants  with PHGs. This health risk information  is appended to the
ACWA guidelines.

2.O California  Drinking  Water  Regulatory  Process

California Health and Safety Code Section 116365 requires the State to develop a PHG
for every contaminant  with a primary drinking water standard or for any contaminant  the
State is proposing  to regulate with a primary drinking water standard.  A PHG is the
level of a contaminant  in drinking water that poses no significant  health risk if consumed
for a lifetime. The process of establishing  a PHG is a risk assessment  based strictly on
human health considerations.  PHGs are recommended  targets and are not required to
be met by any public water system.

The State office designated  to develop PHGs is the California  Environmental  Protection
Agency's  Office of Environmental  Health Hazard Assessment  (OEHHA).  The PHG is

 then  forwarded  to the State  Water  Resources  Control  Board,  Division  of Drinking  Water
(DD\/V)  for  use  in  revising  or  developing  a Maximum  Contaminant  Level  (MCL)  in
drinking  water.  The  MCL  is the highest  level  of a contaminant  that is allowed  in drinking
water.  State  MCLs  cannot  be less stringent  than federal  MCLs  and must be as close  as
is  technically  and  economically  feasible  to  the  PHGs.  DDW  is  required  to  take
treatment  technologies  and  cost  of compliance  into  account  when  setting  an  MCL.
Each  MCL  is reviewed  at least  once  every  five years.

Two  radiological  contaminants  (gross  alpha  particle  and gross  beta particle)  have  MCLs
but  do  not  yet  have  designated  PHGs.  For  these  contaminants,  the  Maximum
Contaminant  Level  Goal  (MCLG),  the  federal  u.s.  Environmental  Protection  Agency
(USEPA)  equivalent  of PHGs,  is used  in the 2022  PHGs  Report.

3.O Identification  of Contaminants

Section  116470(b)(1)  of the  Health  and  Safety  Code  requires  public  water  systems
serving  more  than  10,000  service  connections  to identify  each  contaminant  detected  in
drinking  water  that  exceeded  the  applicable  PHG.  Section  116470(f)  requires  the
MCLG  to be used  for comparison  if there  is no applicable  PHG.

The  City of  South  Gate  (City)  water  system  has  approximately  14,289  service
connections.  The following  constituents  were detected  at one or more  locations  within

 The City operates  one Spray Aeration  Treatment System installed in the South  Gate
Park Reservoir for the treatment of PCE and TCE detected in the local groundwater.

Arsenic  - The BATs for removal  of arsenic in water for large water systems  are:
activated  alumina,  coagulation/filtration,  electrodialysis,  ion exchange, lime soffening,
oxidation/filtration,  and reverse osmosis.  Arsenic was detected above the PHG in the
local groundwater.  The City is in compliance  with the MCL for arsenic.  The estimated
cost to reduce arsenic levels in local groundwater  to below the PHG of O.004 microgram
per liter (pg/l) using ion exchange was calculated.  Because the DDW detection limit for
purposes of reporting (DLR) for arsenic is 2 pg/1, treating arsenic to below the PHG level
means treating arsenic to below the DLR of 2 pg/1. There are numerous  factors that
may influence the actual cost of reducing arsenic levels to the PHG.  Achieving  the
water quality goal for arsenic  could  be approximately  $6,410,000  per year,  or $448  per
service connection  per year.

Gross Alpha and Uranium  - The only BAT for the removal of gross alpha in water for
large water systems is reverse osmosis, which can also remove uranium, if detected.
Gross alpha was detected above the MCLG in the local groundwater.  Uranium was
detected  above the PHG in the local groundwater.  The cost of providing  treatment
using reverse osmosis to reduce gross alpha levels in local groundwater  to the MCLG of
0 picoCurie  per liter (pCi/l) (and consequently  uranium in local groundwater  below the
PHG) was calculated.  Because the DLR for gross alpha is 3 pCi/1, treating gross alpha
to 0 pCi/l means treating it to below the DLR of 3 pCi/1. Achieving the water quality goal
for gross alpha could range from $1,440,000  to $12,300,000  per year, or between $10I
and $864 per service connection per year.

PCE and TCE - The BATs for removing  PCE and TCE in water are granular activated
carbon (GAC) and packed tower aeration (PTA).  PCE and TCE were detected above
their respective  PHGs in the local groundwater  and above the PHG for PCE in the
treated  water from the City's Spray Aeration  Treatment  System.  The City is in
compliance  with the MCL for PCE and TCE. The estimated  cost to treat PCE and TCE
in the local groundwater  to below the PHG of O.06 pg/1 using PTA was calculated.
Because the DLR for PCE and TCE is O.5 pg/1, treating PCE and TCE to below their
respective  PHGs means treating PCE and TCE to below the DLR of O.5 pg/1. There are
numerous  factors that may influence the actual cost of treating PCE and TCE levels to
their respective  PHGs.  Achieving  the water quality goal for PCE and TCE using PTA
could range from $751,000  to $1,990,000  per year,  or between $53  and  $139  per

 Whatare  Drinking  WaterStandards?
 The U.S Environmental  Protection Agency (USEPA) limits the amount of certain substances allowed in tap water.ln California, the StateWater
 Resources Control Board (State Water Board) regulates tap water quality by enforcing limits that are at least as stringent as the Federal EPA's.
 Historically, California limits are more stringent than the Federal ones.

 There are two types of these limits, known as standards. Primary standards protect you from substances that could potentially  affect your
 health. Secondary standards regulate substances that affect the aesthetic qualities of water. Regulations set a Maximum Contaminant  Level
 (MCL) for each of the primary and secondary standards.The  MCL is the highest level of a substance that is allowed in your drinking water.

 Public Health Goals (PHGs) are set by the California Environmental  Protection Agency  (EPA). PHGs provide more information  on the quality
 of drinking water to customers, and are similar to their federal counterparts,  Maximum  Contaminant  Level Goals (MCLGs). PHGs and MCLGs
 are advisory levels that are nonenforceable.  Both PHGs and MCLGs are concentrations  of a substance below which there are no known or
 expected health risks.

How DolRead  the Water Quality  Table?

 Although we test for over 100 substances, regulations require us to report onlythose found in your water.The first column ofthe water quality
 table lists substances detected in your water. The next columns list the average concentration  and range of concentrations  found in your
 drinking water. Following are columns thatlistthe  MCL and PHG or MCLG,if appropriate.The  last column describes thelikely sources of these
 substances in drinking water.

 To review the quality of your drinking water, compare the highest concentration  and the MCL. Check for substances greater than the MCL.
 Exceedence of a primary MCL does not usually constitute  an immediate  health threat. Rather, it requires testing the source water more
 frequently for a short duration. If test results show that the water continues to exceed the MCL, the water must be treated to remove the
 substance, or the source must be removed from service.

 The sources of drinking water (both tap water and bottled water) include rivers, lakes, streams, ponds, reservoirs, springs and wells. As water
 travels over the surface of the land or through the ground, it dissolves naturally occurring minerals and, in some cases, radioactive  material
 and can pick up substances resulting from the presence of animals or from human activity.

 Standards  Code has been adopted  by the State Building  Standards  Commission  and published  in
 the California  Code of Regulations,  Title  24 ("2022  Building  Standards  Code").

 State law mandates that California jurisdictions  enforce the 2022 Building Standards Code,
effective January 1, 2023, for all new building constructions in California. While the California
Building  Standards Commission adopts building code standards to be used statewide,  City
Council action to adopt these codes at a local level is also part of the code adoption process.
Adoption of these codes by the City allows for the inclusion of administrative provisions  and
limited  amendments to the state codes. State law permits local jurisdictions  to make
modifications  to the state codes that are reasonably necessary  because of local conditions
provided the City makes express findings that the changes are needed because of climatic,
geologic or topographic conditions. The proposed Ordinance contains the adoption of these
codes and administrative provisions for the enforcement of the codes. The Ordinance makes
findings  regarding local geographic, climatic  and topographic  conditions that make the
amendments to the state codes reasonably necessary for building construction in the City.

In accordance with state law, the 2021 edition of the Uniform Swimming Pool, Spa and Hot Tub
Code and the 2021 edition of the Uniform Solar, Hydronics and Geothermal Code were adopted
by the State Building Standards and published by the International Association of Plumbing and
Mechanical  Officials.

Administrative  provisions of the California Building Standard Codes are adopted and include
past amendments carried forward as recommended by the City's Building  Official. Such
amendments include provisions regarding permits, fees, inspections, completion of residential
remodeling and Board of Appeals proceedings. The City has not made any amendments to
building, residential, plumbing and electrical codes for over twelve years. The sections for the
numerical order for the proposed ordinance have changed to match the format of the 2022
California  Code of Regulations;  the context has not changed. A Summary of existing
amendments carried forward are provided as Attachment B.

BACKGROUND:  The state's Building Standard Codes have been subject to a series of major
transformation since the 2001 International Code Council (ICC) model codes were introduced.
The 2022 State Codes utilize the most up to date code documents which have been developed
through a national code development process. These construction codes include the California
Administrative,  Building,  Residential, Electrical, Plumbing, Mechanical, Energy, Historical
Building, Existing Building, Reference standards and Green Building Standards as well as other
related  codes.

Adoption of Ordinance No. 2022-10-CC incorporates the 2022 Building Standards Codes and
the 2021 International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials (IAPMO) codes which
will keep the City's building regulations consistent with those of the State. They provide
minimum standards to safeguard life or limb, health, property and public welfare. The proposed
Ordinance is necessary to keep us in compliance with State regulations while allowing the City
to properly address special local conditions.

ENVIRONMENTAL  ASSESSMENT:  Environmental  review is not required under the
California  Environmental  Quality  Act (CEQA)  pursuant to CEQA Guidelines  Sections
15060(c)(2) (the activity will not result in a direct or reasonable foreseeable indirect physical
change in the environment) and 15060(c)(3) (the activity is not a project as defined in Section
15378), Title 14, California Code of Regulations, because adoption of the proposed Ordinances
has no potential for resulting in a physical change to the environment, directly or indirectly.

  SUBJECT:  RESOLUTION  TO  ADOPT  THE  2017  UPDATED  GREATER  LOS
  ANGELES  INTEGRATED  REGIONAL  WATER  MANAGEMENT  PLAN  TO  PURSUE
  GRANT  FUNDING

  PURPOSE:  The City  is applying  for a grant for water  system  improvements.  As a prerequisite
  of the application,  the City  must adopt  a Resolution  approving  the adoption  of the 2017 Updated
  Greater  Los  Angeles  County  Region  Integrated  Regional  Water  Management  Plan  (GLAC
  IRWMP).

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider  adopting  a Resolution  of the
  2017 Updated  Greater  Los Angeles  Integrated  Regional  Water  Management  Plan (GLAC  IRWM)
  Plan for the South  Gate Water  Main  Replacement  Program.

  FISCAL  IMPACT:  None.  There  are no funding  commitments  associated  with  this item.

  ANALYSIS:.  The  State  of  California  Department  of  Water  Resources  (DWR)  created  the
  Integrated  Regional  Water  Management  (IRWM)  Program  to  encourage  integrated  regional
  strategies  for  managing  water  resources  and  to  provide  :tunding  for  both  planning  and
  implementation  of projects  that supportmanagement  of water  supply,  water quality,  environmental
  interests,  drought  protection,  flood  protection,  and reduction  of dependence  on imported  water.

  The City is participating  in a collaborative  process  to pursue  grant funding  of regionally  significant
  projects.  The  South  Gate  Water  Main  Replacement  Project,  with  a construction  value  of
  $2,300,000,  is under  consideration.  The grantor,  DWR  requires  that applicants  to adopt the latest
  region's  IRWM  Plan. Adopting  the IRWM  plan does not cornrnitthe  City to any specific  objectives
  within  the plan itself.

  BACKGROUND:  The City  is a member  of a large  watershed-based  coalition  called  the Los
  Angeles  Gateway  Region  Integrated  Regional  Water  Management  Joint  Powers  Authority
  ("GWMA").  It is currently  comprised  of 25 cities,  three water  agencies  and the Port of Long Beach
  that  are collectively  responsible  for  coordinating  the regional  watershed  needs  of two  million
  people  in the Gateway  Region  located  in Southeastern  Los Angeles  County.  To increase  its funding
  opportunities,  GWMA  became  a member  of  the  countywide  Greater  Los  Angeles  County
  Integrated  Regional  Water  Management  ("GLAC  IRWM").  The GLAC  IRWM  is comprised  of

  1
  68
 the five  Sub-Regions  that span from  Ventura  County  to Orange  County,  including  portions  of both
counties,  and  from  the  Pacific  Ocean  coastline  to the  San  Gabriel  Mountains.  The  Region
represents  approximately  nine million  people.

The  GLAC  IRWM  Plan  identifies  a comprehensive  set of solutions  to achieve  the following
objectives  over a 25 year planning  horizon:  (1) reduce the Region's  reliance  on imported  water;
(2) comply  with  water quality  regulations  by improving  the quality  of urban runoff,  (3) stormwater
and wastewater;  (4) protect,  restore  and enhance  natural  processes  and habitats;  (5)  increase
watershed  friendly  recreational  space for all communities;  (6) reduce  flood  risk  in flood  prone
areas by  either  increasing  pro  a  a
approaches;  and (7) adapt to and mitigate  against  climate  change vulnerabilities.

Adopting  the 2017 Updated  GLAC  IRWM  Plan will enable GWMA  to apply for the existing and
future  grant funding  under  various  grant programs.  Due to the size of the document,  a link to the
complete  GLAC  IRW  Plan is available  at https://dpw.lacounty.gov/wmd/irwmp/.

  SUBJECT:  AMENDMENT  NO.  l  TO  CONTRACT  N0.  2020-96-CC  FOR
  GROUNDWATER  PUMPING  WATER  RIGHTS  LEASE  AGREEMENT  BETWEEN
  THE CITY OF SOUTH GATE  AND THE  CITY OF CERRITOS

  PURPOSE:  Amending the current lease agreement with the City of Cerritos to extend the
  term for an additional two years, which will generate revenue for the Water Fund which can be
  used for infrastructure improvements to benefit customers in South Gate.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a.  Approving Amendment No. 1 to contract No. 2020-96-CC ("Amendment  No. 1") for
  Groundwater Pumping Water Rights Lease Agreement with the City of Cerritos to lease
  1,000 acre-feet of the City of South Gate's unused water rights, annually, for a two-year
  term effectiveJmy  1, :).023; and
  b.  Authorizing  the Mayor  to execute the Agreement  in a form  acceptable  to the City
  Attorney.

  FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no fiscal impact to the General Fund. Amendment No. l will
  generate revenue in the amount of $190,000 each fiscal year for a total of $380,000 for the two-
  year term.

  ANALYSIS:  The City can lease its iu'iused water rights. Annually, the City has 11,183 AF of
  water from the adjudicated APA and a water demand of 8,300 AF, leaving an estimated 2,883
  AF of unused water rights aru"iually. Unused water rights cargover  annually but the unused
  water rights are subject to lapse if the balance exceeds 6,210 AF. Currently, the City has a
  projected balance of over 3,138 AF of unused water rights.

  A Request for Proposal ("RFP") was issued to competitively select lease agreements on June 23,
  2022, and no bids were received. However, the City of Cerritos agreed to amend the existing
  contract and extend the lease for two more years with the same terms. Staff is recommending
  amending the contract with the City of Cerritos extending the term at the same rate of $190 per
  AF.

  SUBJECT:  AGREEMENT  WITH  HYDROSCIENTIFIC  WEST TO PROVIDE  AS-
  NEEDED  TECHNICAL  SUPPORT  SERVICES  FOR THE SUPERVISORY  CONTROL
  AND DATA ACQUISITION  (SCADA) SYSTEM OF THE CITY'S MUNICIPAL  WATER
  SYSTEM

  PURPOSE:  To approve an Agreement with HydroScientific  West ("HSW") for a two-year
  term for as-needed technical support services. The City utilizes the services of a consultant for as-
  needed technical support services of the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition  (SCADA)
  System.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:
  a.  Approving  an Agreement with HydroScientific  West for as-needed technical support
  services for the Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) system, for a two-
  year term with an option to extend up to two years, for an amount not-to-exceed  $30,000,
  annually; and
  b.  Authorizing  the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable to the City Attorney.

  FISCAL IMPACT:  There is no impact to the General Fund. The total amount of the Agreement
  is $60,000, which is $30,000, annually, for atwo-year period, and will be funded with Water Funds
  budgeted  in Account No. 411-731-71-6101.

  ANALYSIS:  The City utilizes the services of HSW for as-needed technical support services for
  the SCADA System under Contract No. 3377 which was set to expire on September 30, 2022. On
  September 13, 2022, the City Council extended the contract on a month-to-month  basis, for up to
  six months, to provide time to issue a Request for Proposal ("RFP") to procure a new contract. The
  RFP has since been issued and only one proposal was received; and it was from HSW.

  Staff is recommending proceeding with awarding a new contract to HSW, for a two-year term with
  an option to extend the contract up to two years. The proposed contract will commence effective
  December 1, 2022, and will expire on November 30, 2024, unless extended by the City Council.
  The proposed budget is $30,000, annually.

  Continuing the service agreement with HSW provides the following  benefits: 1) having installed
  the current SCADA system in 2013, HSW has detailed knowledge  of the system unique to the

  1
  116
 City;  2)  contracting  with  the  current  service  provider  will  minimize  any  software  security
concerns;  (3)  reasonable  fees;  (4)  a licensed  CIO  Electrical  Contractor  and certified  system
integrator;  and (5) a proven  track record  of troubleshooting  complex  technical  iSsues by the service
provider.

BACKGROUND:  The  City's  municipal  water  system  is a complex  network  of  facilities
consisting  of ten water  wells,  four booster  pump  stations,  four reservoir  sites, and over 135 miles
of water distribution  pipelines.  One of the tools utilized  to manage  and operate  the water  system's
facilities  is laiown  as the SCADA  system.  The SCADA  system  is a software  and hardware  program
that provides  the ability  to operate  water  facilities  remotely,  in real-time,  from  a central  computer
station  located  at the City's  Corporate  Yard.  SCADA  software  and hardware  is installed  at the
location  of several  water  facilities.  That said, the SCADA  system  is a vital  component  of the water
system.

The  SCADA  System  requires  regular  maintenance,  troubleshooting,  software  and  hardware
upgrades,  and technical  support  of the type  that  is common  to any  computer-based  system.
Technical  support  is also required  after infrastructure  upgrades  are completed,  such as, to install
or integrate  new components  to the SCADA  system.

On August  30, 2022,  an RFP for the engineering  services  was sent to five  firms.  On October  17,
2022,  City  Clerk's  Office  received  one proposal  submitted  by HSW.

The proposed  Agreement  provides  the following  technical  support  services:

  *  Troubleshoot  instrumentation  and hardware  to rectify  system  issues.

  *  Install  new control  components  and hardware  as directed  by the City  staff.

  *  Upgrade/enhance  existing  monitoring  systems  at remote  sites to supplement  capital  projects.

  @  Ensure  so'Jiware  updates  on a continuous  basis. Provide  continuous  remote  assistance.

  *  Meet  with  City  staff  and other  support  contractor  to ensure  the integrity  of the SCADA
  System.

Located  in the City  of Escondido,  HSW  is a reputable  company  in water  facility  maintenance  and
rehabilitation.  HSW  has the necessary  technical  expertise,  and experience  to provide  the City  as-
needed  emergency  repairs  and major  maintenance  services.

HSW's  performance  record  with  the  City  has met  expectations.  They  have  provided  similar
services  for purveyors  such as the City  of Pico Rivera,  Metropolitan  Water  District,  United  States
Bureau  of Reclamation,  and Kern  Water  Bank Authorities.

m.  BACKGROUND

The City's  municipal  water system is a complex  network  of facilities  consisting  of eight active
water wells, three standby water wells, four booster pump stations, four reservoir  sites, and over
135 miles of water distribution pipelines.

The City's  water system serves the approximately  90 percent; Golden State Water Company  serves
the Hollydale  area; and Tract 180 Mutual  Water Company  and Walnut  Mutual  Water Company
serves a few properties  in the City.  There are over 14,500  custoiner  accounts  that the City  is
servicing including residential, commercial and industrial customers.  The City also has several
recycled water service connections to serve mainly landscape irrigation.

Currently,  the City's  potable water demand is met by eight active wells (see Figures 1 and 2, and
Table 1). The annual production  is approxii'nately  8,300 acre-feet  and the City  has an Allowed
Pumping  Allocation  (APA)  of 11,183.  Three additional  wells (Well  No. 13, 23, and 25) in the
system are classified standby at present due to elevated levels of iron, inanganese,  or other volatile
organic carbon (VOC) contaminants as classified by EPA.

Well No. 28 and 29, located at Ardmore  Avenue,  are primary  production  wells for the west side
of the City.  Well No. 26 and No. 27, located at Tweedy  Boulevard,  serves south west portion  of
the City.  Wells No. 13 (standby),  14, 18, and 19, located in the South Gate Park on the east side

Reservoir and area east of Los Angeles River.

The water extracted  from all groundwater  wells is disinfected  with  liquid  sodium  hypochlorite  at
the well  facilities  prior to the delivery  into the distribution  systei'n. Currently,  there is wellhead
treatment  at two facilities  of the water system for removal  of primary  and secondary contaminants:
l) Spray Aeration  Treatment  Systems for Park Well No. 13, 14, 18, and 19 to remove  VOC;  and
2) Loprest  Greensand  Treatment  Plant for Well No. 27 at the Westside  Reservoir  site to rei'nove
Iron and Manganese.  These two systems have been operating  successfully  for many  years  on a
continuous basis.

There are five, at grade, steel water tanks and one underground  concrete tank in the system with a
total capacity  of 14 MG. Two of the at grade tanks, capacity  2.5 MG each, are located at Firestone
Boulevard  and the I-710 Freeway,  referred  to as the Hawkins  Reservoirs,  while  the two at grade
tanks, capacity 1.66 MG each, at Westside Reservoir  site are located at Tweedy  Boulevard  between
Well No. 26 and Well No. 27.  The recently  coinpleted  Elizabeth  Reservoir  has a capacity  of 1.8
MG.  The underground  concrete tank, capacity  4.2 MG, is located in the South Gate Park.

The water systei'n has two MWD  connections,  CB-7 and CB-11,  in the City (See Location  Map).
The City has not used MWD water for several years and currently anticipates  using the connections
only for major emergencies. In addition, the City water system has five  interconnections  with
neighboring  purveyors  for  mutual  assistance  in a supply  shortage.  Although  all these five
interconnections  are bi-directional,  the City  is the intended  provider.  The City  currently  has
sufficient  pumping  rights  to supply  their  residents  and sell water to the neighboring  agencies.
Regardless,  these  interconnections  may  provide  the essential  backup  supply  needed  during
emergencies.

One of the tools utilized  to manage and operate the City  water system facilities  is  the SCADA
systein. The SCADA  system provides  the ability  to operate water facilities  remotely,  in real-time,
from a central  computer  station  located  at the City's  Corporate  Yard,  as well  as through  laptop
computers assigned to operators.  SCADA  software  and hardware  is installed  at the location  of
several water facilities.

The existing SCADA  system was originally  installed in 2013. City plans to upgrade SCADA
software and hardware as part of its Capital Improvement  Programs to be implemented in the near
future. The proposed project  will  replace  software  and hardware  currently  not supported  to
properly update the system.

The Consultant  shall write  control  logics  and prograi'ns  to operate the City water system control
components  sucl'i as programmable  logic  controllers  (PLC's),  data radios,  operator  interface
terminals (OIT's),  and the water control human  machine  interface  (HMI)  using  the City's
ClearSCADA  software on an as-needed basis.

 Agreement,  the fiscal  impact  to the General  Fund will  be approximately  $85,012  for Police,  traffic  plan
 implementation,  and Public  Works  Department  personnel  overtime.

 ANALYSIS:  The Fair features  carnival  rides,  entertainment,  games,  and food  vendors.  The proposed
 Agreement  specifies  the roles,  responsibilities  and expectations  of all parties  related  to the Fair.  All
 impacted  departments  have  reviewed  the  Agreement,  and  with  only  one  (l)  exception,  have  not
 requested  any  substantive  changes,  the Agreement  essentially  remains  the same as in prior  years.

 The one exception  is the elimination  of a contingency  that, should  the Fair  expenses  exceed  revenues,
 the City  would  be responsible  for up to an additional  subsidy  of $10,000  (which  would  result  in the
 City  receiving  $20,000  in total reimbursement,  instead  of the customary  $30,000).

PURPOSE:  To consider entering into a Professional Services Agreement with Helpline  Youth

RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City Council will consider:

  Emergency Rental and Utility Assistance Program;  and
  b.  Appropriating  $245,000 from the American Rescue Plan fiinds to an account determined by

from the City's allocation of American Rescue Funds recently received from the U.S. Treasury

Taking all the above into consideration, staff concluded that both organizations are technically,
historically, and professionally qualified to provide emergency rental and utility services required by
the Request For Proposal. With City's CDBG funded assistance, HYC assisted 21 households in 2019,
72 households in 2020, and five households in 2021 for a total of 98 households. Due to their proposal
and established history of providing  emergency rental and utility assistance to the South Gate
community, staff is recommending that the City Council award the agreement for the South Gate
Emergency Rental and Utility Assistance Program to HYC.

For their implementation  of the program identified in the RFP, HYC will be paid an hourly rate of
$39.66 per hour, for an amount not-to-exceed  $82,500, annually. Additionally, HYC will be
reimbursed for the direct emergency rental and utility assistance they provide eligible South Gate
residents for an amount not to exceed $162,500, for a combined annual total not to exceed $245,000.
The term of the agreement will commence December 1, 2022, and conclude on November 30, 2023,
with the possibility of two, one-year extensions.

BACKGROUND:  On October 26,2021, the South Gate City Council authorized the City Manager
to utilize ARPA SLFRF funding from the United States Department of Treasury for the Revive South
Gate Spending Plan, which includes five spending categories: recovery from the pandemic, direct
assistance programs, public health and safety, critical infrastructure, and city fiscal health. To respond
to needs locally, the City of South Gate will consider allocating $245,000 annually for an emergency
rental and utility assistance program from ARPA funding, with two one-year possible extensions. The
$245,000 is inclusive of direct assistance for liouseholds (an amount not to exceed $6,000 per
household) and a fully burdened rate to cover all costs associated with the program implementation.
In-person assistance will be offered at City Hall two days a week from 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. at the
Community  Development  Department  public  counter.

FY 2022

In response  to the COVID-19  crisis,  the City of South  Gate,  is seeking  one or more  contractors  to
administer  an Emergency  Rental  and  Utility  Assistance  Program  (Program)  to aid low-income
renters  who  are unable  to pay their  rent  due  to the  COVID-19  public  health  emergency.  The
Program  will provide  short-term,  emergency  utility  and  rental  assistance  to low-income  renters
using  federal  American  Rescue  Plan Act (ARPA)  Funding.

Proposals  are  due  by Wednesday,  September  21, 2022,  by 4:00  PM.  Proposals  may  be
mailed,  hand  delivered,  or emailed  by the  due date  and  time.

 Overview
The American  Rescue  Plan Act of 2021  (ARPA)  was established  to help states  and
localities  address  the economic  and health consequences  of the COVID-19  public health
emergency  and its economic  impacts.  Since the start of the COVID-19  pandemic,  risk of
homelessness  has increased. This Tunding opportunity provides support to community
organizations  that are responding  to these public health and economic emergency
impacts.  The  awarded  applicant  will enter into an agreement  with the City of South Gate
to deliver  an emergency  rental and utility assistance  program  to eligible  City residents.
The awarded  contract  will be for u  to  245 000  r  ear  inna  November  I  2022
with the possibility of two, one-year extensions.  The $245,000 is inclusive of direct
assistance for households (an amount not to exceed $6,000 per household) and a fully
burdened rate to cover all costs associated with the program implementation.

Background
Globally  and nationally,  the COVID-19  pandemic  has negatively  affected  low-income
households' ability to maintain their rental and utility payment obligations. As a result of
these pandemic  related issues, on March 11, 2021, President Biden signed the American
Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (H.R. 1319) into law. The ARPA provides $1.9 trillion in
additional relief to respond to the novel coronavirus (COVID-19). According to the u.s.
Department of the Treasury, the Coronavirus  State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds
(SLFRF) provide a substantial infusion of resources to help turn the tide on the COVID-
19 pandemic,  address  its fallout,  and lays the foundation  for a strong  and equitable
reCoVery.

ARPA  includes  direct  assistance  to cities to address  the negative  public  health  and
economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic, including approximately  $34.5 million to
the City of South Gate ("ARPA Funds"). The City of South Gate coordinated a process of
community  engagement  which  included  listening  sessions,  meetings  with community
partners  and  businesses,  an online  survey  tool,  and  City Council  and  Commission
meetings  to tiear what South Gate residents  supported  as funding  priorities.  One of the
key themes that arose from this process was a need for rental and utility relief assistance.

On October 26, 2021, the South Gate City Council authorized  the City Manager  to utilize
ARPA  SLFRF  funding  from the United  States  Department  of Treasury  for the Revive
South Gate Spending Plan, which includes five spending categories: recovery from the
pandemic, direct assistance programs, public health and safety, critical infrastructure, and
City Fiscal health. To respond to needs locally, the City of South Gate has authorized  the
expenditure of up to $245,000 annually for an ARPA funded rental and utility assistance
program, with two one-year possible extensions.  The $245,000 is inclusive of direct
assistance for households (an amount not to exceed $6,000 per household)  and a fully
burdened rate to cover all costs associated with the program implementation.

on ARPA spending.  Key links and information  on reporting  requirements  and spending
categories  are listed below.

  SUBJECT:  ACCEPTANCE  OF  PROJECT  COMPLETION  AND  NOTICE  OF
  COMPLETION  FOR THE PARK  MAINTENANCE  YARD REROOFING  PROJECT,
  CITY PROJECT  NO. 691-PRK

  PURPOSE:  Construction of the subject project is complete and the retention payment to the
  contractor is due. Section 7107 of the Public Contract Code requires the City to accept
  completion of the project and issue public notice of such, prior to releasing the retention
  payment.

  RECOMMENDED  ACTIONS:  The City  Council  will  consider:
  a.  Accepting  completion of construction  of the Park Maintenance  Yard Reroofing  Project,
  City  Project No. 691-PRK; and
  b.  Directing  the City Clerk to file the Notice  of Completion  with the Los Angeles County
  Registrar  Recorder's  Office.

  FISC AL IMP ACT:  There is no impact on the General Fund. The final construction contract
  amount is $107,065, inclusive of Contract Change Orders No. l and No. 2, and it was :tunded
  with California National Resources Agency Grant Funds from Account No. 524-460-61-9100.
  The total project budget is $196,000. The project expenditures are summarized below.

 ANALYSIS:  Construction of the Park Maintenance Yard Reroofing Project is complete,  and
staff is preparing to process the final payment for construction services to Best Contracting
Services, Inc. Public Contract Code establishes requirements that the City must abide to prior to
releasing the final payment for construction projects. The Notice of Completion provides written
notice to concerned parties that all work on the project has been completed. The Notice  of
Completion initiates the 35-day period within which concerned parties may exercise their lien
rights for the work they performed on the project. The City may use a part or all the 5% retention
payment to settle any liens exercised against the City. If no liens or claims have been filed within
35 days of the filing of the Notice of Completion, the City will release the retention and any
remaining  amount  due to the contractor.

BACKGROUND:  The Park Maintenance Yard Reroofing Project is a part of the City's
Capital Improvement Program. The project included the replacement of deteriorated corrugated
metal roofing and removal of asbestos containing mastic in the old roofing.

On January 26, 2021, the City Council approved a purchase order contract ("PO No. 6318") for
Best Contracting Services, Inc. ("Best"), in the amount of $121,000, to construct the Park
Maintenance Yard Reroofing Project. On May 11, 2021, the City Council ratified a revised
purchase order contract with Best Contracting Services, Inc., in the amount of $97,498, revising
the scope of work. The original scope of work called for the removal of the existing cormgated
metal roof on the garage portion of the building and replacement with plywood decking and
installation of TPO type membrane roofing. Due to structural concerns with the garage portion of
the building, it was decided to replace the corrugated metal roof in kind, so as not to increase the
roof weight. The scope of work on the remaining portion of the building that houses a
lunchroom, storage, and office space was not changed from TPO membrane roofing over the
existing  built-up  roofing.

Construction  has been completed  and City representatives  inspected and approved  the
improvements. All work was performed in accordance with the revised project scope of work,
with acceptable quality and workmanship.  In addition, the project required a building permit
from the Community  Development  Building  & Safety Division.  Best has met all contract
obligations. The City Council may now accept the project as complete. The Notice  of
Completion can now be filed with the Los Angeles County Registrar Recorder's Office.

Two change orders were administratively  approved for the project.  Contract Change Order No.
1 was for inflationary cost increases of materials for $4,691. Change Order No. 2, for $4,877,
was for the abatement of asbestos mastic found in the roof mastic. The original contract amount
was $97,498. The final amount is $107,065 inclusive of Change Order No. 1 and 2.

BACKGROUND:  The Urban  Orchard  Project  is a part of the Capital  Improvement  Program.
Now  under  construction  is the installation  of a new passive  park on a 7-acre  site located  at 9475
W,  Frontage  Road.  This  site  is  located  between  Firestone  Boulevard  to  the  north,  the
Thunderbird  Villa  Mobile  Home  Park to the south,  the Los Angeles  River  to the west and I-710
Freeway  to the east.

On May  25, 2021,  the City
  Council approved Contract No. 2021-66-CC  with NR Development,
Inc.,  in the amount of $15,870,853.  Construction  began on August 2, 2021 and is scheduled for
completion  in spring 2023. To date, four change orders have been approved  administratively
totaling  $331,639,  and one has been approved  by City Council  in the amount of $415,968  as
follows:

  *  In November  2021,  the Contract  Change Order No. I in the amount  of $95,314,  was
  administratively  approved to strengthen the park lighting foundation.

  *  In  February  2022,  Contract  Change  Order No. 2 in the amount  of $97,656  was
  administratively  approved  to add additional  a vault and switch equipment  required  by
  Southern  California  Edison ($51,440),  remove and dispose of unforeseen  concrete slabs

  ($32,950).

  *  In April  2022, Contract Change Order No. 3 in the amount of $65,040 was
  administratively  approved to modify the improvements  along the east perimeter road
  ($28,325), remove and dispose of unforeseen concrete slabs ($32,007), for unforeseen
  labor and material for additional pipe penetrations not identified in the plans ($3,255) and
  for unforeseen labor and material to protect the liner from the wetland sidewall ($1,453).

  *  InMay2022,ContractChangeOrderNo.4,intheamountof$415,968,wasapprovedby
  the City Council to address unforeseen field conditions related to handling,  hauling  and
  disposal of excavated soils.

  *  In August 2022, Contract Change Order No. 5, in the amount of $73,629 was
  administratively  approved to correct and increase the grades in the playground area by 5
  feet, revising a concrete walking path, landscape, and irrigation modifications ($36,114),
  to improve the Bandini Channel chain-link fence and access ladder to meet Los Angeles
  County Flood Control requirements ($8,612), remove and dispose of unforeseen debris
  encountered in the shade structure on Time and Material basis ($764), place a protective
  seal coating on two pedestrian bridges ($1,937), and for soil sampling, inspections,

Although  the project has experienced a number of change orders, it is proceeding under budget.

Construction of the park is scheduled for completion in spring 2023. To date, the following
improvements  have been completed:  rough grading, drop inlet for storm water diversion
structures from the Bandini Channel, a wetland overlook area, a flowing stream adjacent to the
education/flexible  space building and wetland, bioswale, construction of 18 raised planters,
planting of 75 trees, installation of two shade structures to promote prolonged hours and use of
the park, a water element at the playground,  and the installation of multi-use walking and
bicycle pathways, exercise equipment located at various stages along the walking and bicycle
paths, benches, picnic tables, drinking fountains, trash cans, and pathway lighting.

SUBJECT:  ORDINANCE  AMENDING  SECTION  1.04.065 (SALARY  OF MEMBERS  -
COMPENSATION),  OF CHAPTER  1.04 (CITY COUNCIL),  TITLE l (ADMINISTRATION
AND PERSONNEL),  OF THE SOUTH GATE MUNCIPAL  CODE INCREASING  THE CITY
COUNCIL  SALARY

PURPOSE: To introduce an Ordinance amending the municipal code for the salary compensation  of
the City Council, in accordance with California Government Code, and restating all benefits for South
Gate Elected  Officials  to a single  document.

RECOMMENDED  ACTION:  The City Council will consider waiving the reading in 'full and
introducing an Ordinance amending Section 1.04.065 (Salary of Members - Compensation),  of
Chapter 1.04 (City Council), of Title I (Administration and Personnel), of the South Gate Municipal
Code  increasing  the City  Council  salary

FISCAL  IMPACT:  The total aru"iual cost for the changes to the City Council compensation will be
$1,680 annually per Council Member and $8,400 total for all five members, aru"iually. In addition, the
City Treasurer's salary is tied to that of City Council per Section 1.05.065 (City Treasurer  -
Compensation) which voters approved in November 2000. The total increase costs for all six elected
positions will be $10,080, annually.

ANALYSIS:  California Goverent  Code Section 36516 (a) (4), establishes the amount elected city
Council members can received in salai'y. Based on municipal population, the state law established a
base level and permitted annual increases of up to 5%. However, salary changes cannot go into effect
until after a municipal election at which City Council members are elected, per Goverru'nent Code
Section 36516.5. The City Council compensation was last adjusted in 2017, which became effective
after the March 14, 2017, regular municipal election. The compensation amount was raised from $600
per month to $650 per month, regardless of the number of City Council meetings held a month.

Based on the Government Code Section limiting annual adjustments, the attached Ordinance would
adjust the current $650 per month salary to $790 per month. This Ordinance will only affect the salary
of the City Council  Members and the City Treasurer.

  l

  437
 At a Special Municipal Election on November 7, 2000, the voters of the City of South Gate approved
the addition of Section 1.05.065 to the Municipal Code which limited and tied the salary for
  the
position of City Treasurer to that which the City Council members receive on a monthly basis. Thus,
the City Treasurer currently receives $650 per month and, if this Ordinance is adopted,
  the
compensation for this position would also be increased to $790 per month.

The Ordinance also restates the benefits for all Elected Officials in South Gate under Attachment A to
consolidate the total compensation for these positions in one location. The schedule of benefits that
were previously stipulated in Resolutions No. 7808 (City Clerk) and No. 7751 (City Council/City
Treasurer) are included in Attachment A to allow for a more transparent approach by listing the total
compensation  of Elected  Officials  for South  Gate.

BACKGROUND:  In 2010, Government Code Section 36516.5 became effective and established
statewide salary levels for City Council members in cities. Those levels were broken into five
population categories and South Gate fell under the cities with populations between 75,000 and
150,000. The limit, at that time, was $600 per month. As stated, the law provided for up to 5% annual
adjustments and any adjustment could only occur after a municipal election where City Council seats
were on the ballot.

The $600 per month salary remained in effect until March 2017, when it was raised to $650 per month
under Ordinance No. 2335. If approved, this Ordinance would adjust the monthly salary for City
Council Members according to the stipulated limits in Governrnent Code Section 36516.5 (a) (4).

regulations  at the time.

For the City  Clerk,  a "dollar  for dollar"  benefit  shall be provided  which  matches  the City  Clerk's
voluntary  contribution  into the City's  457 deferred  compensation  plan, subject  to the terms of said
plan and Internal  Revenue  Service  regulations.  For purposes  of this benefit,  the City  shall match
the  City  Clerk's  contribution  in  the  City's  457  deferred  compensation  plan,  provided  such
matching  sum does not exceed  50% of the maximum  regular  contribution  limit,  excluding  Special
457 catch-up  contributions.  Said regular  contribution  limit  shall be adjusted  from  time to time by
the IRS.

Auto  Allowance:  It is recognized  that  elected  officials  attend  various  community  meetings
outside  the Civic  Center/City  Hall,  participate  in regional  and state organizations,  and travel  to
conferences/seminars.  Therefore,  the City  shall  provide  for  the use of the  elected  official's
personal  automobile  to conduct  such City  business  at the rate of $500 per month  (an increase  of
$25),  which  shall  be taxable  as compensation.  Elected  officials  shall  not  be eligible  for
reimbursement  of milage  for use of their personal  automobiles.

Communication  Allowance:  The City  shall reimburse  the elected  official  for the use of his/her
personal  communication  device  to conduct  City business  at the rate of $100 per month,  which  shall
be taxable  as compensation.

Fitness  Benefit:  Elected  Officials  shall receive  a free membership  at the South Gate Sports Center
which  will  include  privileges  for a spouse and legal dependents  for immediate  family  members.

Duration:  These  salary  and benefits  shall remain  in full  force  and effect  until  such time  as they
are amended  by  the  City  Council  by  subsequent  resolutiorffordinance  and/or  any  state  law
requirements.

minutes_text:
CITY OF SOUTH GATE
  REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING
  MINUTES
  TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 22, 2022
CALL TO ORDER  Al Rios, Mayor called a Regular City Council Meeting to order at 6:30
  p.m.
INVOCATION

PLEDGE OF
ALLEGIANCE  Gregory Martinez, City Treasurer

ROLL CALL  Yodit Glaze, City Clerk

PRESENT  Mayor Al Rios, Council Member Maria Davila, and Council Member Gil
  Hurtado; City Treasurer Gregory Martinez, City Attorney Raul F. Salinas

ABSENT  Vice Mayor Maria del Pilar Avalos, Council Member Denise Diaz, and
  City Manager Chris Jeffers

RECESS  The City Council recessed the Regular City Council Meeting of November
  22, 2022, to a Recessed Regular City Council Meeting of November 29,
  2022, by motion of Council Member Hurtado and seconded by Council
  Member Davila.

  ROLL CALL: Council Member Davila, yes; Council Member Hurtado,
  yes; Mayor Rios, yes

1
PERSONNEL RECRUITMENT
& SELECTION  The City Council considered receiving and filing the list of new and
  promoted full-time employees hired or promoted during October 2022.

2
WATER  The City Council considered conducting a public hearing to receiving and
  filing the City of South Gate 2022 Public Health Goals Report to meet the
  requirements of the California Health and Safety Code.

CONSENT CALENDAR  Agenda Items 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are Consent Calendar Items.
3
MUNICIPAL CODE ADMIN The City Council will consider waiving the reading in full and
  adopting Ordinance No. 2022-10-CC amending certain chapters and
  sections of Title 9 (Buildings) of the South Gate Municipal Code by
  adopting by reference the 2022 California Codes of Regulations, Title 24
  ("2022 Building Standards Code") and the 2021 International Association
  of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials Codes.
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF NOVEMBER 22, 2022

4
WATER  The City Council will consider adopting a Resolution of the 2017 Updated
  Greater Los Angeles Integrated Regional Water Management Plan (GLAC
  IRWM) Plan for the South Gate Water Main Replacement Program.
5
SOLID WASTE MGMT  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving Amendment No. 3 to Contract No. 2021-70-CC with
  HF&H Consultants, LLC., for solid waste management services
  necessary to complete the transition to UWS services and for services
  that are necessary for compliance with state regulations, in an amount
  not-to-exceed $86,784;

  b. Authorizing the appropriation of $133,384 from the Refuse Fund
  balance to Account Number 413-733-51-6101 as necessary to fund
  transition and solid waste management expenditures through the end
  of Fiscal Year 2022/23; and

  c. Authorizing the mayor to execute the Amendment No. 3 in a form
  acceptable to the City Attorney.

6
WATER  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving Amendment No. 1 to Contract No. 2020-96-
  CC ("Amendment No. 1") for Groundwater Pumping Water Rights
  Lease Agreement with the City of Cerritos to lease 1,000 acre-feet of
  the City of South Gate's unused water rights, annually, for a two-year
  term effective July 1, 2023; and

  b. Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable
  to the City Attorney.
7
WATER  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving an Agreement with HydroScientific West for as-needed
  technical support services for the Supervisory Control and Data
  Acquisition (SCADA) system, for a two-year term with an option to
  extend up to two years, for an amount not-to-exceed $30,000,
  annually; and

  b. Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable
  to the City Attorney.

  Page 2 of 4
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF NOVEMBER 22, 2022
8
COMMUNITY
PROMOTION  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving an Event License Agreement ("Agreement") with the
  Tweedy Mile Association to produce the Annual Tweedy Street Fair
  Festival ("Fair") for a term of three years; an

  b. Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable
  to the City Attorney.
9
EMERGENCY/DISASTER
PLANNING/PROGRAMS  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving an Agreement with Helpline Youth Counseling, Inc., to
  implement the South Gate Emergency Rental and Utility Assistance
  Program; and

  b. Appropriating $245,000 from the American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA)
  funds to an account determined by the Director of Administrative
  Services to fund the South Gate Emergency Rental and Utility
  Assistance Program; and

  c. Authorizing the Mayor to execute the Agreement in a form acceptable
  to the City Attorney.
10
PARKS  The City Council will consider:

  a. Accepting completion of construction of the Park Maintenance Yard
  Reroofing Project, City Project No. 691-PRK; and

  b. Directing the City Clerk to file the Notice of Completion with the Los
  Angeles County Registrar Recorder's Office.
11
STREETS/SIDEWALKS/
LANDSCAPING  The City Council will consider:

  a. Approving Change Order No. 6 to Contract No. 2021-66-CC with NR
  Development, Inc., to fund additional work required to complete
  construction of the Urban Orchard Project, City Project No. 539-PRK,
  in a budgetary amount of $288,019;

  b. Authorizing the Assistant City Manager/Director of Public Works to
  execute Contract Change Order No. 6; and

  c. Approving an increase to the City Manager's authority to
  administratively approve change orders from a cumulative total of
  $500,000 to a cumulative total of $750,000.
  Page 3 of 4
   REGULAR CITY COUNCIL MEETING MINUTES OF NOVEMBER 22, 2022

12
MINUTES  The City Council will consider approving:

  a. The Regular Meeting minutes of September 27, 2022; and

  b. The Special Meeting minutes of October 11, 2022.

13
CITY COUNCIL  The City Council will consider waiving the reading in full and introducing
  an Ordinance amending Section 1.04.065 (Salary of Members -
  Compensation), of Chapter 1.04 (City Council), of Title I (Administration
  and Personnel), of the South Gate Municipal Code increasing the City
  Council salary.

14
WARRANTS  The City Council will consider approving the Warrant Register for
  November 22, 2022.

  Total of Checks:  $2,380,075.63
  Less: Voids  $  (706.10)
  Less: Employee Payroll Deductions  $ (438,492.77)
  Grand Total:  $1,940,876.76

  Cancellations: 98605, 99006, 95288, 97909, 98092, 98225

ADJOURNMENT  Council Member Hurtado adjourned the meeting at 6:35 p.m. and
  seconded by Council Member Davila.

PASSED and APPROVED this 28th day of March 2023.

Maria del Pilar Avalos, Mayor  Yodit G aze, City Clerk
